title: I’m a non-programmer solo dev who made a Steam demo using vibe coding and AI-assisted game development
author: DoubleJayM
selftext:
https://reddit.com/link/1syy89r/video/21rl2owao4yg1/player



Hi everyone,

I’m a non-programmer solo developer working on **BROKEN SOUL : Boss Rush**, a 2D soulslike boss rush action game focused on pattern reading, dodging, parrying, and challenging boss fights.

I recently released the Steam demo, and I wanted to share it here because this project was made almost entirely through an AI-assisted “vibe coding” workflow.

I don’t come from a traditional game development or programming background. Instead, I used AI as a development partner throughout almost every part of the project.

AI was actively used for:

* Game planning and system design
* JavaScript / HTML5 implementation support
* Debugging and code review
* Combat mechanics and boss pattern iteration
* UI/UX ideas and structure
* Sprite, illustration, and visual direction prompts
* Text, localization, store page copy, and marketing materials
* Development workflow planning as a solo creator

I tried to use almost every AI tool that could realistically help in a one-person development environment — coding assistants, image generation tools, writing tools, translation tools, design prompts, and planning workflows.

That said, the game itself is not an “AI gameplay gimmick.”  
It is a handcrafted 2D action game where the player learns boss patterns, dodges attacks, parries at the right moment, and survives through timing and repetition.

The most interesting part of this project was learning what AI can and cannot replace.

AI helped a lot with speed, structure, iteration, and turning ideas into working features.  
But game feel, difficulty tuning, readability, balance, and whether combat actually feels fair still required manual testing, judgment, and repeated adjustment.

https://preview.redd.it/pdpibvrco4yg1.png?width=4398&format=png&auto=webp&s=4e3ecf6bb03d9972b3b57e072debeaf858a7cca4

  


Steam page / Demo:  
[https://store.steampowered.com/app/4424450/BROKEN\_SOUL\_\_Boss\_Rush/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4424450/BROKEN_SOUL__Boss_Rush/)

I’d love to hear from other AI-assisted game developers.

For those using AI in your own projects:  
How far do you think a non-programmer can realistically go with vibe coding and AI tools in game development?

comments.author: Smilysis
comments.body: Nice sprite animations! which model/workflow did you use to achieve this fluidity?

replies.author: DoubleJayM
replies.body:
Thanks! It wasn’t done with a single model or one-click workflow.

The general workflow was AI-assisted sprite generation + a lot of manual iteration. I usually start by defining key poses first — idle, wind-up, attack, hit frame, recovery — then generate sprite sheets while keeping the front-facing view, weapon position, and silhouette consistent.

After that, I clean up the frames manually, adjust spacing/timing, remove broken frames, and test the animation directly in-game. Most of the fluidity comes from adding enough in-between frames and making sure the motion has clear anticipation, impact, and recovery.

So the short version is: AI helps me create and iterate the frames faster, but the timing, readability, and final polish still require a lot of manual checking.

comments.author: TheSuperSteve
comments.body:
I'm making my own AI-assisted game as well, and you showcasing your game is very motivating for me. I gave you a wishlist, and I wish you lots of luck with your project! 

Did you use AI for the music as well, did you hire someone or buy a music pack? Just curious!

replies.author: DoubleJayM
replies.body:
Thank you so much! I really appreciate the wishlist, and I’m glad my project could be motivating for you.

For the music, I also used an AI-assisted workflow. I didn’t hire a composer or buy a music pack. I used AI tools to create the initial music direction and tracks, then selected and adjusted them based on the game’s mood and battle pacing.

Since I’m working as a solo dev, I tried to use AI across almost every part of the project — planning, coding, visuals, localization, marketing, and music as well.

That said, music still needs a lot of human judgment. Even if AI can generate tracks quickly, I still had to choose what actually fits the scene, whether the loop feels natural, and whether the track supports the tension of the boss fight.

Good luck with your AI-assisted game too! I’d love to see what you’re working on when you’re ready to share it.

replies.author: TheSuperSteve
replies.body:
I am using AI music in my project as well, and I was curious about how other devs source their music. Thanks for letting me know. Like you, I'm carefully selecting melodies, editing stems in Audacity, and I'm writing lyrics (and asking AI how I can improve them) for my lyrical tracks. 

I plan to showcase my game eventually, but I'm not ready to show it yet. Again, good luck with yours!

replies.author: DoubleJayM
replies.body:
That sounds like a really thoughtful workflow.

I think AI music still needs a lot of human direction, especially when it comes to choosing the right melody, cleaning up stems, matching the track to the scene, and making sure it doesn’t feel generic. Using Audacity and refining lyrics yourself sounds like a good way to keep some personal authorship in the process.

  
Good luck with your project too. I hope I get to see it when you’re ready to showcase it!

comments.author: AethericPulse
comments.body:
For the short cinematic with the character that looks like Malphite from league of legends, what did you use to make that cinematic?
I'm about 2 months into developing an AI-assisted game also and my biggest fear are the cinematics I will have to deal with. 
Also, I constantly see wishlist trading, is there any benefit to wishlists if the person won't end up buying the game? Asking since I'm not close to that stage and wondering if it's pushed more based on wishlists or something

replies.author: DoubleJayM
replies.body:
For the short cinematic, I used an AI-assisted workflow rather than a traditional cinematic pipeline.

The rough process was: define the scene direction first, create visual prompts based on the character/monster concept, generate short visual/cinematic shots, then manually select, edit, and adjust the usable results to match the game’s mood. It still needs a lot of human judgment, especially for consistency, pacing, and making sure it doesn’t feel disconnected from the actual game.

Cinematics are definitely one of the harder parts of AI-assisted game dev. AI can help generate impressive shots, but keeping the same character, style, camera language, and emotional tone across multiple shots is still difficult.

replies.body: What tool did you use for the cinematic? Was it video AI like seedance or something?

comments.author: HealthyWest6482
comments.body: Playing it right now because our projects are similar, the lane system might be exactly what I need. The combat feel is nice - don't let the obvious unintelligible luddie 'feedback' discourage you. The better your project gets, the more threatening/offensive it is to them.

replies.author: DoubleJayM
replies.body:
Thank you, that means a lot.

The lane system came from trying to make boss patterns readable while still keeping the combat tense. I wanted the player to focus more on timing, pattern recognition, dodge/parry decisions, and positioning rather than free movement complexity.

I’m glad the combat feel is coming through. I also appreciate the encouragement. I’m trying to take useful criticism seriously, but not let the noise stop the project.

replies.author: HealthyWest6482
replies.body:
I understand where you're coming from completely. balancing tension and readability are definitely keynotes to engaging combat. ok now lets make it so when she takes damage, its visible through articles of clothing falling off.

I think one big upgrade thats probably low cost big improvement is to author a dedicated movement string for the MC. dodging and parry reads super clean because the flow of movement reconciles with the action feedback itself, but the most basic action (z) has them moving forward swinging it reads kinda janky - so imagine a sprinting/backstep playback before the damaging swing instead.
